newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity closes up amid warming weather.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity closes up amid warming weather.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures closed higher in anticipation of increased air conditioning demand in the Southwest as temperatures begin their seasonal climb, market sources said Thursday.
"The market's been up and down all day, but the overall trend seems higher," said one dealer.
She cited short-covering as well as expectations of increased Southwest power demand as contributing to the market's bullish tone.
Concerns that inflows to hydroelectric dams in the Northwest have yet to pick up speed also lent support to the complex, traders said.
May Palo Verde closed 56 cents higher at $16.45 per megawatt hour (MWh) after trading as high as $17.50, while June settled up 57 cents at $17.50 after reaching as high as $18.25.
Other active PV contracts gained 10 to 30 cents per MWh.
May California Oregon Border (COB) closed up 30 cents at $13.29 per MWh, compared with a high for the day of $13.40, while June was up 33 cents at $12.88.
Other COB contracts were up 20 to 35 cents a MWh.
NYMEX estimated 367 COB and 1,266 PV contracts traded.
Electricity futures were also seen drawing some strength from natural gas futures, with May NYMEX Henry Hub natural gas futures closing up 6.4 cents at $2.069 per million British thermal units.

Temperatures in the Southwest were forecast as high as 12 degrees F above normal through the weekend and above normal for the six to 10-day outlook, while the Northwest was expected to see readings four to 12 degrees above normal over the next five days.

For the month of May, the National Weather Service forecast above-normal temperatures over Washington state, the western half of Oregon, California, the southern half of the Great Basin, most of New Mexico and southwest Texas during May.
For May-July, above-normal temperatures were forecast for California, southwest Arizona, western Nevada and northern Washington.
In California, the 1,080 megawatt (MW) San Onofre 3 nuclear power unit remained shut for refueling and maintenance, with an expected restart date in late June.

The 1,158 MW WNP-2 nuclear plant in Washington state was also shut for refueling, and was expected to resume power output in early July, while the 1,087 MW Diablo Canyon nuclear unit 1 in California was expected to begin a 36-day refueling outage on Saturday.
In addition, nearly 6,000 MW of thermal generating capacity was off-line in the West for planned and unplanned maintenance as well as hydropower displacement sales.
